newsitem.title: UK: Prince Charles admits he has failed UK monarchy.
newsitem.headline: Prince Charles admits he has failed UK monarchy.

text.p: Prince Charles was reported on Monday as admitting to failing the British monarchy and vowing to "sort the whole bloody mess out" by reaching out more to ordinary people.

His remarks, reported by a friend, were published on the eve of a live television debate on the royal family and a new opinion poll showing that less than half of Britons believe the country will still have a monarchy in 50 years time.
Charles's public standing plummetted during the acrimonious break-up of his marriage to popular Princess Diana and his confession of adultery with Camilla Parker Bowles.
Charles and Diana, who had two sons, Prince William, 14, and Prince Harry, 12, divorced last year.
"I've done a lot of things wrong and I've been so for too long, I've let the queen down, my family -- including William and Harry -- and Camilla," Charles said.
"I've let down the whole institution of the monarchy. I've even failed Diana," the Mirror quoted him as saying. It said Charles's remarks were relayed by one of his closest friends.
The paper said Charles, 48, who is seen as distant in comparison to his warm-hearted ex-wife, was determined to put things right.
"Nothing will happen overnight. But from now on Charles will make a sustained effort to work for others, particularly the royal family.
"His aim will be to be more positive and to reach out to more ordinary people," it quoted the friend as saying.
The Mirror story appeared as Charles was on a skiing holiday with his son Harry in the Swiss resort of Klosters.
Diana, who took a separate holiday on the Caribbean island of Barbuda, has announced a visit next week to Angola to meet victims of landmines.
A MORI poll commissioned for Tuesday's television debate on the future of the monarchy showed the size of the task facing Charles.
Only 46 percent of those questioned thought he would make a good king, while 36 percent said he would be a bad king.
Some 48 percent thought Britain would not have a monarchy in 50 years time and 68 per cent said the scandals of recent years had harmed the image of the royal family.
Queen Elizabeth has sought to placate increasingly hostile Britons by agreeing to pay income tax and opening up Buckingham Palace to the public. Her 70th birthday last year was particularly low-key.

But her efforts have been overwhelmed by scandals involving Charles and Diana, both of whom have admitted adultery, and the Duchess of York, known as Fergie, who has failed to live down the shame of being photographed topless with her American "business adviser" sucking her toes.
